doc.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021

title: Businessman's bounce and making people feel good
summary: How the two-beat businessman's bounce gets reluctant dancers moving before the band moves to swing.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Is that because you played it as a businessman’s bounce?
Well I made a record called “Businessman’s Bounce.”
I know you did that’s why I asked.

And it stemmed from the term musicians used to use back in those days, and so it’s hard to explain how things, how different things were back — a musician back in those days knew that his job was to make people feel good. And the people would, when they walked, be it a country club or a juke joint or a jazz club or whatever, people walked into a club or wherever you were playing, and they’d worked hard all week long and they would come in with almost like a challenge and it was like, “Make me feel good.” That was — and you knew that that’s what your job was. So say for instance if you’re playing a dance or a country club the whole thing was okay get the people out on that dance floor. And you’d play a tune and then sometimes they’re reluctant and resistant. So they would sit there. And so, “Okay what do we play?” And so we’d try and think, “Let’s play ‘Stardust’.” And then he’d say, he’d call a tune and he’d say, “Businessman’s Bounce.” Which was like a two-beat [scats]. And most people can count to two. And they would get out on the dance floor and they’d move one foot on this beat and one foot on this beat, and the next thing you know they thought they were dancing. And at some point you would make people swing who had no intentions of swinging and didn’t know what swinging was, but when they got set then they know that it felt good. So that was pretty much the psychology of the deal.
Yeah I love it when you do that and somewhere after they get started you switch to 4/4 —

Oh yeah, yeah. I’m trying to think of this one tune of Cannonball’s. And that’s, not just, you know not just the musicians who really knew how to take people on the journey, they knew how to do that. And it would evolve. It would start, like I say [scats] — and then eventually two-spot. But eventually it turned into a circle to where it was like what it’s all about.
